summary: Specifies a restricted profile of Internet mail protocols for exchanging voice messages between voice processing server platforms. It sets a minimum common set of features for interoperability. It obsoletes RFC 2421 and RFC 2423.

eli5.summary: Voicemail boxes from different companies need to pass messages to one another. This sets the common basics so they can.

questions: how do voicemail systems exchange messages over smtp
what audio format does vpim use
subtitle: A restricted profile of Internet mail that lets voice mail machines from different makers swap voice messages.

tldr.problem: Voice messaging systems were special-purpose machines that networked over analog protocols, and they lacked many facilities of normal Internet mail computers, so there was no common digital way to connect them.
tldr.mechanism: VPIM v2 restricts and extends Internet mail: messages travel by ESMTP and are packaged as a Multipart/Voice-Message MIME container holding 32 kbit/s ADPCM audio, optional TIFF-F fax and forwarded messages, with simple numeric addresses and machine-parsable status reports.
tldr.outcome: It defines the minimum common set of features so conforming systems can interwork. It obsoletes RFC 2421 and changes no protocol, only describes version 2 more precisely.

facts.label: Typical address limit on voice machines

today: RFC 3801 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 2421 and RFC 2423, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. The text says no protocol changes were made from RFC 2421, and that it merges in the Multipart/Voice-Message definition from RFC 2423.

sections.title: Why a Voice Profile for Mail
sections.content:
RFC 3801 defines the Voice Profile for Internet Mail (VPIM) version 2. It is a restricted profile of the Internet multimedia messaging protocols for use between voice processing server platforms. These platforms were historically special-purpose computers that interface to a telephone switch, and they often lack the facilities of a traditional Internet email computer. VPIM therefore also specifies extra functionality where it is needed.

Messages between such machines used to travel by analog networking based on DTMF signaling and analog voice playback. VPIM gives them a standard digital protocol built on MIME and the existing mail transport. The design goal is to make as few restrictions and additions to Internet mail as possible, so proven mail software can be reused.

The RFC lists typical limits of voice mail machines: text is rarely displayed, the machine acts as one combined mail agent and store with little relaying, distribution lists are usually only local aliases, error reports must be machine-parsable so they can be voiced over the phone, and addresses are generally 16 or fewer numeric characters.

VPIM is meant for exchanges between voice messaging systems, and between them and VPIM-aware clients. It is not intended or optimized for downloading to or sending from commercial email clients. The separate Internet Voice Messaging effort covers that case.
sections.eli5: Old voicemail boxes only had buttons and a phone speaker, so they could not read normal email. This RFC says how to wrap a voice message in an email envelope that those boxes can still handle.

sections.title: Addresses and Special Mailboxes
sections.content:
VPIM addresses use the RFC 822 form based on the Domain Name System: a local part that names the mailbox and a host part that names the machine. The local part is a US-ASCII string. Because most voice mail networks rely on the telephone keypad, short numeric local parts SHOULD be used, although letters and long identifiers are permitted.

The local part falls into four groups: a plain mailbox number, a mailbox number plus an extension, a + followed by an international number, and an international number plus an extension. International numbers follow E.164 with a maximum of 15 digits, and the leading + flags a public telephone number. An example is +16137637582@vm.nortel.ca.

Two special addresses are reserved. A mailbox named postmaster MUST exist on every system for diagnostics. The address non-mail-user is used as the originator when a reply is not possible, such as a telephone answering message. A conforming system MUST NOT permit a reply to it, and a message addressed to it MUST be rejected with status code 5.1.1, Mailbox does not exist.

Distribution lists are optional. A system MAY support them as simple aliases, and when it cannot list every recipient it SHOULD omit the recipient header fields rather than show a partial list.
sections.eli5: Voicemail addresses look like phone numbers, because that is what you can type on a keypad. A special address says this message came from an answering machine, so do not try to reply.

sections.title: Message Header Fields
sections.content:
VPIM allows a fixed set of header fields and gives separate send and receive rules for each. Systems MUST be able to accept and ignore header fields they do not know.

  • From MUST be present with the originator's full address, ideally with a personal name. It is shown as the originator and used for replies.
  • To and Cc MAY be sent when all recipients are known, and receivers MAY discard them if they cannot store them. A blind-copied recipient MUST NOT appear in the disclosed list.
  • Date MUST report when the message was sent, with a time zone that SHOULD be a four-digit offset such as -0500.
  • Message-Id MUST be globally unique and is used when sending a message disposition notification.
  • Reply-To SHOULD NOT be sent, because voice mail systems typically support only one originator.
  • Received MUST be added by a conforming system and MUST NOT be removed when relaying.
  • MIME-Version MUST be present, and systems SHOULD add the comment (Voice 2.0).
  • Subject SHOULD be generated, with a generic value such as Voice Message for systems that have no text interface.

The Sensitivity field carries Personal, Private or Company-Confidential. Only Private has VPIM semantics: a receiver MUST prohibit forwarding it, and if the system cannot assure privacy it MUST send a negative delivery notification with status 5.6.0. The Importance field takes low, normal or high.
sections.eli5: The header is the front of the envelope: who it is from, when it was sent and a unique number. A Private stamp means the receiver must not pass the message on to anyone else.

sections.title: Voice, Fax and Other Contents
sections.content:
A VPIM message is a Multipart/Voice-Message MIME container. Its meaning is identical to Multipart/Mixed, so systems that do not know it can treat it as Multipart/Mixed. It needs a boundary parameter and a version parameter, whose value is 2.0 for this specification. Conforming systems MUST use it in a VPIM message and MUST send only the profiled content types inside it: Audio/*, Image/* and Message/RFC822.

Voice is sent by default as Audio/32KADPCM, a moderately compressed encoding at 32 kbits/second. Spoken names and subjects are expected to be about 5 and 10 seconds. Receivers MUST decode it. If a system can handle only one voice body, multiple bodies SHOULD be concatenated in order and MUST NOT be discarded.

Fax uses Image/TIFF in the TIFF-F profile, with one image strip per page and the parameter application=faxbw in outbound messages. Systems that cannot render fax SHOULD keep the voice and drop the fax.

Each audio part MUST carry a Content-Disposition of inline with a voice parameter that says what the audio is. Text/Directory SHOULD NOT be sent and Text/Plain SHOULD NOT be sent inside the container. Proprietary codecs SHOULD NOT be used unless the sender expects the recipient to accept them. Optional fields include Content-Description, Content-Duration in seconds and Content-Language.

Forwarded messages SHOULD be sent as a Message/RFC822 part inside the container, with the annotation in a separate Audio or Image part. Replies to messages that cannot be answered, such as telephone answering messages, SHOULD NOT offer a reply option.
sections.eli5: A voice message is a box with labeled slots: the spoken message, maybe the sender saying their name, maybe a fax page. The labels tell the receiver which slot holds what, and the usual sound format is one every machine knows.

sections.title: Delivery and Disposition Notifications
sections.content:
Because callers can only listen, error reports must be machine-parsable. A conforming system MUST be able to send and receive Delivery Status Notifications (DSNs), and unless requested otherwise a non-delivery DSN MUST be sent whenever a message is not delivered. A DSN SHOULD carry a spoken delivery status in its human-readable part, though a text status is allowed. If the return path is null (<>), as with a call answer message, DSNs MUST NOT be sent.

Message Disposition Notifications (MDNs) report what happened after a message reached the mailbox, such as played or deleted unheard. Systems SHOULD support requesting MDNs with the Disposition-Notification-To header and SHOULD respond to such a request. Appendix C and D of the RFC give example status codes and dispositions, for instance a mailbox that does not exist maps to 5.1.1 and a mailbox over quota to 4.2.2.

When a system receives an Audio or Image type it cannot store or render, it MUST return the message to the originator with a notification saying the media is not supported.
sections.eli5: When a voicemail cannot be delivered, the sending machine gets a note back saying why, and the note can be read out loud over the phone. Another kind of note can say the message was played.

sections.title: Transport with ESMTP
sections.content:
VPIM messages move between voice mail machines over the Internet Extended Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (ESMTP). All delivery information, such as the sender and recipient addresses, travels in the ESMTP dialog as the message envelope, which corresponds to the control block of analog voice protocols. A conforming system MUST implement all mandatory SMTP and ESMTP commands.

Support for the SMTP service extensions is graded by how much it matters. The efficiency extensions (SIZE, BINARYMIME, PIPELINING) can be dropped on a downgrade without changing what the sender or recipient sees. The functional extensions (DSN and ENHANCEDSTATUSCODES) are essential, so DSN support is needed at every hop between sender and recipient. If a relay must forward without the DSN request, it is RECOMMENDED that it keep trying to deliver, but it MUST send a delivery status notification to the originator.

When binary transport is available, audio and fax SHOULD be sent as Binary. Otherwise they MUST be encoded as Base64. Receivers MUST decode Binary, 7bit, 8bit, Base64 and Quoted-Printable.

Voice systems with only a telephone interface must map a dialed number to a routable fully qualified domain name, by implementation-specific means. SNMP SHOULD be supported for management.
sections.eli5: The messages ride the same postal system as normal email. Because a voice message is big, the machines tell each other its size first, and they send back notes about whether it arrived.

sections.title: Two Kinds of Conformance
sections.content:
The RFC defines two areas of conformance: transport and content. A transport-conformant system passes VPIM messages in a store-and-forward manner, with assured delivery notifications and without losing information. A content-conformant system generates and interprets VPIM messages: it honors the profile's restrictions when sending, and when receiving it can handle all VPIM content types and gives the right notification for contents it cannot render.

Voice messaging systems and protocol conversion gateways are end systems and are expected to be both. Relay systems are expected to be transport-conformant, but they must also create VPIM-conforming delivery status notifications when delivery fails. Desktop email clients that support VPIM are expected to be content-conformant. Appendix A of the RFC summarizes the requirements in a table.
sections.eli5: Some machines only carry the mail, like postal trucks, and others open and read it, like the person at the door. Each kind has its own rules to follow.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
VPIM is a profile of existing Internet mail, so any security should be part of the Internet security infrastructure rather than a new mechanism. The RFC says it creates no security issues beyond those already in the profiled protocols, and it covers only the extra threats from joining the two services.

  • Spoofed sender: the real sender may differ from the Sender or From fields or the envelope address. SMTP gives no inherent sender authentication, though recognizing the sender's voice may help.
  • Unsolicited voice mail: giving a voice mailbox an Internet address opens it to unsolicited voice or text messages, and voice mail users expect more mailbox privacy.
  • Message disclosure: users expect more privacy than plain Internet mail gives, and that expectation SHOULD be preserved as far as possible.

The profile does not prevent using any Internet object or channel security protocol to encrypt or authenticate messages.
sections.eli5: Anyone can write a fake name on an envelope, and a mailbox that had a private phone line is now reachable by strangers. The fix is to use the normal security tools of Internet mail.
